Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,

  1
 closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 4:00 pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be
summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be
recorded for public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment
due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to
adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

  8
 STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

  SUBJECT:  STATUS UPDATE  ON VACANT  POSITIONS  IN COMPLIANCE  WITH
  CALIFORNIA  GOVERNMENT  CODE § 3502.3

  PURPOSE:  California Governrnent Code Fp3502.3 requires that each public agency present at a
  public hearing at least once per fiscal year the City's vacant position prior to the adoption of an
  annual budget and to permit the City's Associations to make a presentation at the hearing if they
  so desire.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council will consider:
  a. ConductingapublichearingontheCity'svacancies;and
  b.  Receiving  and filing  the status update report on vacancies in compliance  with California
  Government  Code F>3502.3.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There is no fiscal impact  from  receiving  the report  on the presentation  of
  vacant  positions

  BACKGROUND:  Governor Newsom signed Assembly  Bill  2561 (AB2561)  into law on
  September 22, 2024, to amend the Meyers-Milias-Brown  Act (MMBA).  AB2561  added
  California Government Code E>3502.3, which requires public agencies to hold a public hearing at
  least once per fiscal year to report on vacancy and recruitment status and retention efforts. A
  basis for the new requirements is that the California Legislature determined that vacancies  are
  widespread and can result in significant problems in the public sector. As vacancies  increase,
  existing employees are then required to take on heavier workloads, which results in burnout and
  increased turnover. This, in turn, could negatively impact and diminish the delivery of needed
  public  services.

  To this  end, California  Governinent  Code  Ffi 3502.3  imposed  three requirements  on local
  agencies:

  (1) At least once each fiscal year and prior to the adoption of its annual budget, the City
  Council must hold a public hearing and receive the City's report on the status of
  vacancies and recruitment and retention efforts;

  I

  10
   (2) During  the liearing,  the City  must identify  any necessary  changes  to policies,  procedures,
  and recruitment  activities  that may lead to hiring  obstacles;  and
  (3) The City  must allow  the recognized  employee  associations  to make a presentation,  if they
  so  desire.

The City  has five recognized  employee  Associations:  Division  Management  Association  (DMA),
Professional  Mid-Management  Association  (PMMA),  Municipal  Employees'  Association
(MEA),  Police  Management  Association  (PMA),  and the Police  Officers'  Association  (POA).
On  March  18,  2026,  tlie  Human  Resources  Department  notified  eacli  of  the  employee
associations  that  a public  hearing  will  occur  on April  28, 2026,  regarding  the City's  vacancies
and informed  them that they may make a presentation  if they desire.

On March  25, 2026,  notice  of this public  hearing  was published  in the WAVE,  and it has been
continuously  posted  on the City's  website  and outside  aru'iouncement  board  since  March  25,
2026.

The City  has 349 full-time  positions  budgeted  with  52 of these positions  vacant  as of February
24,  2026,  for  an  approximately  14.9%  vacancy  rate.  Attached  to  this  agenda  bill  is  the
PowerPoint  presentation  showing  the number  of vacancies  and percentage  of total  vacancies  by
each City  bargaining  unit.  The Police  Officers'  Association  (POA)  has the highest  vacancy  rate
on  a percentage  basis  at  approximately  21.88%.  The  vacancy  rates  in  the  City's  other
Associations  are: DMA  (O.OO%);  PMMA  (13.73%);  MEA  (15.46%);  and PMA  (O.O%).  The
unrepresented  Executive  Management  Team  is currently  at 14.29%  vacancy.

For Fiscal  Year  2025/26,  the City  has hired  45 new  employees,  23 of which  are full-time,  and
promoted  20 existing  'full-time  employees.  Over  this same period  of time,  the City  received  and
reviewed  1,013  job  applications,  which  is a sharp  decrease  over  the previous  fiscal  year when
2,422 applications  were received.

The  Human  Resources  Department  (HR)  has  established  a thorough  recruitment  process  to
ensure that it can attract  the best possible  candidates.  To do this,  HR in cooperation  with  other
relevant  stakeholders  applies  the following  procedure:

  (1) Reviews  all  job  classification  specifications  (job  descriptions)  and  updates  them  as
  needed  prior  to opening  a recruitment.  Any  modifications  of a job  classification  or the
  creation  of a job classification  goes through  the meet and confer  process  with  the affected
  employee  association.
  (2) Once  the review  of the job  classification  specification  is finalized,  the position  is then
  posted  and  published  on  governrnentjobs.com  and  any  other  applicable  job  board.
  Governrnentjobs.com  is the most  prolific  online  site used by public  agencies  to recruit
  employees  and it is operated  by NEOGOV.
  (3) HR uses an online  tracking  system  to ensure  all candidates  are fairly  and systematically
  reviewed.
  (4) HR  then  pre-screens  all  candidates  to  determine  that  each  meets  the  minimum
  qualifications  for  the position  and  then  organizes  them  from  most  qualified  to least
  qualified  based upon objective,  nondiscriminatory  criteria.
  (5) The  most  qualified  candidates  are then  invited  to  a panel  interview  of  independent
  reviewers,  scored,  and then  objectively  ranked  starting  with  the best  candidate,  from
  which  an eligibility  list is generated.

  2

  11
   (6) HR  will  then  send  to the hiring  authority  the  application  materials  for  the  top  five
  candidates  on the eligibility  list for a final,  subjective  interview  and selection.  The hiring
  authoiity  will  then  contact  HR  infonning  tliem  of the selected  candidate  or identifying
  candidates  for non-selection.
  (7) Once a candidate  is selected,  HR then manages  the negotiation  process  with  the selected
  candidate  until  such time that a conditional  offer  is accepted  or declined  by the candidate.

While  HR dedicates  a substantial  amount  of time into recruiting  the best candidates  for any given
position,  there are substantial  challenges  that the City  faces in this process:

  (1) The local  labor  market  is incredibly  competitive,  and the pool  of qualified  candidates  has
  diminished  over the years when  compared  to pre-COVID  recruitment  efforts.
  (2) The City's  fiscal  health  projects  instability  to prospective  candidates  and causes them  to
  perceive  a high risk in accepting  a position  with  the City.
  (3) Attracting  candidates  located  outside  of  the  local  areas  is challenging  due  to  ever-
  increasing  traffic  congestion  and fuel prices.
  (4) The  Public  Employee  Pension  Reform  Act  (PEPRA)  has disincentivized  employees  to
  remain  at one public  agency  over a career or even remain  in public  sector  employment.
  (5) Although  public  sector  employment  can offer  better  benefits  (e.g.,  medical  coverage,
  pension  eligibility,  etc.)  in some  industries,  private  sector  higher  wages  tend  to attract
  younger  workers  despite  having  little  to no benefits.
  (6) Younger  generations  are not as likely  as their older  generation  counterparts  to remain  tied
  to a singular  employer,  which  causes them to freely  move  from  one employer  to another.
  (7) When  evaluating  candidates'  skill  sets developed  in the private  sector,  such skills  are not
  comparable  or easily  transferrable  to those required  in the public  sector.

Once  hired,  the City  takes  several  efforts  to retain  existing  employees.  For  example,  the City
does generally  offer  a more  competitive  benefits  package  than its competitors,  although  there are
several  larger  cities  that offer  much  higher  wages.  To ensure that the City  remains  competitive,
HR  conducts  a continuous  analysis  of positions  to ensure  that the wages  remain  competitive
within  the relative,  comparative  market  median.  HR evaluates  the City's  positions  to determine  if
they were competitive  with  the market  median  and, in some cases, will  come to City  Council  for
approval  to adjust  the wages  for positions  that fall  below  the accepted  competitive  range.  The
City  also  strives  to  promote  a positive  workplace  culture  with  activities  celebrating  the
employees  such  as  employee  recognition  events,  employee  appreciation  events,  training
opportunities,  and various  support  programs.  However,  due to the City's  current  $9.4 million
structural  deficit,  the  ability  for  the  City  to remain  competitive  in  the  market  may  not  be
sustainable  and, with  the impending  workforce  reduction  that will  likely  result  in layoffs,  it will
be increasingly  difficult  to maintain  positive  morale  in the workplace.

In an effort  to overcome  some of the challenges  the City  is facing  to fill  its vacancies,  the City
and its various  labor  associations  explored  a completely  new  approach  to the  entire  hiring
process  to improve  efficiency,  expand  the pool  of qualified  candidates  for consideration,  and a
"fast  track"  process  to promote  internal  employees  to increase  morale  and retention  efforts.  Last
year,  the  City  Council  approved  replacing  its  antiquated  Civil  Service  Rules  with  the  new
Personnel  Management  Rules.  In doing  this,  the City  implemented  a new  hiring  policy,  which
improved  the efficiency  and efficacy  of the hiring  process.  One of the biggest  improvements  was
the ability  for the City  to quickly  hire qualified  intemal  candidates  in vacancies.

  3

  12
 Additionally,  tlie  City  Manager  implemented  a new  policy  restricting  the use of independent
contractors  except  in  circumstances  where  they  are  absolutely  necessary  and  not  before
notification  is  provided  to  the  impacted  employee  association.  In  many  cases,  motivated
employees  desire  the opportunity  to learn  skills  necessary  to gain  the required  experience  to
advance  to a higher-level  vacancy,  but  in the past,  there  was  no such  pathway  to gain  this
exposure  and experience.  However,  this past fiscal  year and in cooperation  with  the employee
associations,  a Training  & Development  Program  was implemented  to provide  that pathway  for
employees  to gain the experience  necessary  to compete  for a future  promotional  opportunity.  For
example,  the Police  Department  has successfully  used this program  to provide  opportunities  to
Police  Records  Specialists  to promote  into the Police  Dispatcher  position.

For this coming  Fiscal  Year  2026/27,  the biggest  hurdle  the City  will  face to effectively  recruit
and retain  talented  employees,  and to reduce  the  overall  vacancy  rates,  is the  $9.4  million
structural  deficit.  This  deficit  has caused  the City  to implement  a workforce  reduction  plan,
which  is specifically  designed  to "freeze"  positions  when  they do become  vacant  in an effort  to
limit  the actual number  of people  who will  be laid off at the end of this fiscal  year.

BACKGROUND:  The City  of South  Gate has been an annual  recipient  of CDBG  fiinds  since the
enactment  of the Housing  and Community  Development  Act  of 1974.  The  City  is deemed  as an
"entitlement"  jurisdiction  because  it maintains  a population  above  50,000  and meets  certain  other
demographic  criteria.  CDBG  'funding  can be used for a variety  of projects  and programs  primarily
benefiting  persons  of low-  and moderate-income.

The  HUD  regulations  regarding  AAPs  mandate  citizen  participation  and public  review  process,
including  a public  hearing,  prior  to submission.  The draft  Annual  Action  Plan is available  for public
review  and comment  (Attachment  B).  The deadline  to submit  an approved  AAP  is May  15, 2026.

It is important  to note that under  HUD  regulations,  providers  funded  under the Annual  Action  Plan
must meet qualifying  restrictions  unless  part of a designated  category  such as Seniors  or Homeless.
These regulations  include  dociunented  financial  need through  income  tax forms  for example.  It can
also require  the applicant  to hire  contractors  that must  meet various  federal  labor  requirements  and
insurance.  Failure  to adhere to these HUD  regulations  will  mean that expenditures  will  be disqualified,
andthe  City would  needto  reimburse  the federal  funds.  These restrictions  canplace  significant  burdens
on the  subrecipient  to  ensure  they  are followed,  which  can  place  additional  burdens  on them
administratively  which  are not  usually  reimbursable  expenses  or would  be counted  against  the
subrecipient  award.

1.  Introduction

The City of South  Gate's  2026-2027  AAP is based on priorities  established  by the City's  Five-Year
Consolidate  Plan (FY 2025-2029).  The 2026-2027  Action  Plan is the second  year of the City's  FY

2025-2029  Consolidated  Plan and serves  as the City's blueprint  for providing  decent  affordable
housing  to lower-income  households,  providing  suitable  living  environments,  expanding
economic  opportunities,  and expanding  the capacity  of non-profit  housing  providers  to the

residents  of the City of South  Gate. This strategic  plan sets forth  goals, objectives,  and
performance  benchmarks  for measuring  and establishing  a framework  for progress.  The City

will receive  Sl,153,140 in FY 2026-2027 CDBG funds with an additional 534,099 available in
carryover  funds,  for a total  of Sl,187,239.  The City will also receive 5486,118.63 in HOME funds
for FY 2026-2027.  Currently  the City does not anticipate  any additional  HOME carryover  funds

for programming.

The City's Community  Development  Department  manages,  plans, submits,  and implements  the
CDBG and HOME grant  process.  The Department  is involved  in activities  which  enhance

coordination  among  public  and non-profit,  private  housing  providers,  and health  and service
agencies.

2.  Summary  of the objectives  and outcomes  identified  in the Plan Needs Assessment
  Overview

2029 Consolidated  Plan.

  *  Maintain  & Provide  Affordable  Housing
  *  Public  Facilities  & Infrastructure  Improvements
  *  Economic  Development

4.  Summary  of citizen  participation  process  and consultation  process

The City is committed  to maximizing  community  participation  in the CDBG and HOME  planning

process.  To ensure  that  its FY 2026-2027  Annual  Action  Plan was based on resident  needs,  the
City used the following  approach  to create  participation  of residents,  service  providers,  and
other  interested  persons  and organizations:

South  Gate Citizens Advisory  Committee

The South  Gate Citizens  Advisory  Committee  (CAC) is an advisory  board  created  by the City
Council  to ensure  constant  dialog  exists between  the City and the community.  The role of the

CAC is twofold.  First, to ensure  that the City Council  is appraised  of the needs,  desires,  and
interests  of City residents.  Second,  to review  and make recommendations  on CDBG funding  to
the City Council.  The CAC is comprised  of members  representing  the demographic  and social

range  of residents  in the City.  The CAC was actively  involved  in the Annual  Action  Plan process.
The CAC reviewed  and discussed  the 2026-2027  Public Services  applications  and then  made

funding  recommendations  to the City Council  for the Annual  Action  Plan.  It is anticipated  that
the CAC will continue  to serve in an advisory  role in the CDBG process.

Annual  Public Services Application  Process

Leveraqinq

The City and HUD share an interest  in leveraging  HUD resources  to the maximum  extent  that  it
is feasible  to address  priority  needs  and associated  goals.  During  the 5-year  period  of the

Consolidated  Plan the City will seek funds  to leverage  the Federal  CDBG and HOME funds.

Some leveraging  resources  options  are listed  below:

Low-income  Housing  Tax Credit  (LIHTC) - The California  Tax Credit  Allocation  Committee  (TCAC)
facilitates  the investment  of private  capital  into the development  of affordable  rental  housing

for low-income  Californians.  TCAC allocates  federal  and state tax credits  to the developers  of
these  projects.  Corporations  provide  equity  to build the projects  in return  for the tax credits.

Affordable  Housing  Sustainable  Communities  Housing  Program:  AHSC directs  investments  to
historically  under-invested  communities,  giving  more  Californians  access to opportunity.  At

least 50% of AHSC funding  is required  by state  law to be allocated  to affordable  housing  and
projects  in, or that  provide  a benefit  to, disadvantaged  communities.

Housin@ Choice Vouchers:  The South Gate Housing Authority"s  Section  8 rental  voucher
program  provides  rental  assistance  to help very low-income  families  afford  decent,  safe, and

sanitary  rental  housing.  The Housing  Authority  accepts  the application  for rental  assistance,
selects  the applicant  for admission,  and  iSSues  the selected  family  a rental  voucher  confirming

the family's  eligibility  for assistance.  The family  must then  find and lease a dwelling  unit suitable
to the family's  needs  and desires  in the private  rental  market.  The Housing  Authority  pays the
owner  a portion  of the rent  (a housing  assistance  payment  (HAP)) on behalf  of the family.

Mortgage  Credit  Certificate  Program  - Income  tax credits  are available  to first-time  homebuyers
to buy new or existing  single-family  housing.  The County  of Los Angeles  administers  this
program  on behalf  of jurisdictions  in the County.

Matchinq  Requirements

A participating  jurisdiction  (PJ) receiving  HOME funds  is required  to contribute  a 25% match  of
non-HOME  funds  for every  dollar  of HOME funds  spent.  The HOME statute  also provides  a

reduction  of the matching  contribution  under  three  conditions:  1) Fiscal distress,  2) severe  fiscal
distress,  and 3) presidential  disaster  declarations.

Description  of the geographic  areas of the entitlement  (including  areas of low-income  and
minority  concentration)  where  assistance  will  be directed.

HUD funded  activities  are limited  to the City's  low-and  moderate-income  areas or residents.
Areas of the City outside  of the CDBG low-and  moderate-income  areas will benefit  from

activities  that  are limited-clientele  in nature,  i.e., a person/household  can benefit  from  a
federally  assisted  program  provided  they  meet the program's  eligibility  criteria.  Eligibility  is
typically  established  by household  income  and household  size.

CDBG program  funds  will be expended  based on program  criteria.  For example,  public  services
are available  on a citywide  basis for qualified  beneficiaries;  fair housing  and program

administration  activities  will also be carried  out on a citywide  basis.

HOME funds will be utilized towards the rehabilitation of low/moderate income homes.

Rationale  for the priorities  for allocating  investments  geographically

When  determining  the geographic  distribution  where  the City will allocate  their  investments,
City considerations  include  whether  the activity  or program  will physically  be located  within  an
already  designated  CDBG Target  Area, and whether  the program  will directly  benefit  the low-
to-moderate  income  population  in that  area. The City also takes  public  demand,
recommendations  from  City departments,  performance  of previously  CDBG-funded

subrecipients,  recommendations  of other  local entities  like the County  partners  and local non-
profits  into account.

Discussion

An activity  can be designated  as serving  either:  (1) 'Citywide",  or (2) 'in the CDBG

Target  Areas'. "Citywide'  is a designation  used for programs  that  offer  services  to the entire

community.  Many  public  programs  provide  services  to the entire  City, the nature  of these

program  services  is often  to exclusively  serve low-to-moderate  income  people.  If a program  is
designated  as 'CDBG Target  Area'  it is confined  exclusively  to the CDBG Target  Area.

options  in the city. Ways that the City addressed  affordable  housing  needs include  the following
programs:

extremely  low- and low-income  households  through  the South  Gate Housing  Authority's

elderly,  single-parent,  and disabled  special  needs  households.

Introduction

The City is located  within  the Los Angeles  Homeless Services Authority  (LAHSA) Continuum  of
Care. The continuum  provides  oversight  of federal  homeless  assistance  dollars and collaborates
with local communities  to provide  the best service to residents  who are homeless.  The Los
Angeles Continuum  conducts  quarterly  community  meetings,  and when appropriate  the City
attends  and participates  in these meetings.

South Gate residents  who are of low-to-moderate  income  and at risk of experiencing
homelessness  will receive assistance to obtain  and maintain  housing stability  through  CDBG
funded  activities.  Services provided  may include  income  payments  for low-income  eligible
residents,  case management,  and referrals  for housing support.

Describe  the jurisdictions'  one-year  goals and actions  for reducing  and ending  homelessness
including:

  *  Reaching  out to homeless  persons  (especially  unsheltered  persons)  and assessing their
  individual  needs
  The Salvation  Army Bell Shelter operates  a homeless  outreach  program  which consists of
  a mobile  outreach  team.  In coordination  with the South Gate Police Department  Liaison
  and personnel  from the Salvation  Army Bell Shelter street outreach  efforts  by vehicle and
  foot are undertaken.  Street  outreach,  case management,  and referrals  are provided  to
  homeless  families  and individuals  through  this program.  Homeless  clients  are provided
  with guidance  identifying  barriers  to overcoming  homelessness  and developing  a plan to
  address  identified  challenges.  The  team  also  addresses  needs  which  may  include
  accessing  mainstream  services,  increasing  income,  developing  self-determination,  and
  accessing shelter  and housing.

  *  Addressing  the emergency  shelter  and transitional  housing  needs of homeless  persons
  Locally, the Salvation  Army  Bell Shelter  operates  a comprehensive  program  that offers
  transitional  care for up to 350 homeless  men and women.  The goal of the Bell Shelter  is
  to meet the needs of the homeless  population  by addressing  the myriads  of reasons why
  people become  homeless  and assisting them in developing  a higher quality  oflife  through
  independence.  Services  offered  include  emergency  shelter,  transitional  housing,
  substance  abuse  rehabilitation,  case management,  counseling,  on-site  health  care &
  medical  referrals,  HIV/AIDS  education,  ESL classes,  computer  training,  vocational

Introduction

Barriers  to affordable  housing,  as outlined  in the City"s most  recent  Consolidated  Plan, include:

  *  Affordability  concerns  stemming  from  Senate  Bill9  (SB 9) and Assembly  Bill 1033  (AB
  1033)

  *  Extensive  environmental  review  for new developments  required  by the California
  Environmental  Quality  Act (CEQA) which  can delay  housing  projects.

  *  Impacts  on housing  supply  and taxes from  Proposition  13

  *  Impacts  of Article  34 - Voter  for Approval  for Low-Rent  Housing

  *  Transit-Oriented  Development  (TOD) Guidelines

  *  Zoning  policies

Actions  planned  to remove  or ameliorate  the negative  effects  of public  policies  that  serve as
barriers  to affordable  housing  such as land use controls,  tax policies  affecting  land, zoning

ordinances,  building  codes,  fees and charges,  growth  limitations,  and policies  affecting  the
return  on residential  investment.

As a step to address  barriers  to affordable  housing,  the City has updated  its Housing  Element  for
the  2021-2029  planning  period,  identifying  strategies  to conserve  existing  affordable  housing,
provide  adequate  housing  sites,  assist in developing  affordable  housing,  remove  governmental
constraints,  and promote  equal  housing  opportunities.

Addressing  barriers  to  affordable  housing  will  require  ongoing  collaboration  between  local,
regional,  and state  entities  to create  a more  supportive  environment  for  affordable  housing

development.  The City will  continue  to consider  alternate  forms  of residential  development,

including  various  types  of small-lot,  single-family  subdivisions;  mobile  home  parks  that  allow

owner-occupied  spaces;  senior  citizen  multifamily  housing  developments  offering  various
degrees  of care and assistance;  mixed-use  residential,  and planned  unit developments.

Introduction

Outlined  below  are the actions the City will implement  to address the "Other"  sub-strategies  of

Actions  planned  to address obstacles  to meeting  underserved  needs

The primary  obstacles  to meeting  the underserved  needs of low-and  moderate-income  people
include  lack of funding  from federal,  state, and other  local sources, the high cost of housing that
is not affordable  to low-and  moderate-income  people,  and the  lack of availability  of home
improvement  financing  in the private  lending  industry.  To address these obstacles,  the City is
invests HOME funds towards  the construction  of affordable  housing  development.  CDBG funds
are being allocated  to organizations  that provide  public  and neighborhood  services to low-and
moderate-income  people and those with special needs that can help offset other household  costs
that create financial  burdens  for individuals.

Actions  planned  to foster  and maintain  affordable  housing

City also provides  rental  assistance  through  the Housing  Choice Voucher  Program  to very low-
income  households  through  its  Housing  Authority.  The City certifies,  when  available  and
appropriate,  Community  Housing  Development  Organizations  (CHDOs) to provide  affordable
housing  using low HOME rents.

Actions  planned  to reduce lead-based  paint  hazards

All unitsin  a project  assisted with CDBG and HOME funds must comply with the regulations  found
at 24 CFR Part 35. The purpose  of the regulation  is to identify  and address  lead-based  paint
hazards  before  children  are exposed  to  lead.  This  requirement  has been  in effect  since
September  15, 2000.

Lead-based  paint hazards are found  in homes built prior to 1978.  All Grantees  and Participating
Jurisdictions  must  assess homes  built  prior  to 1978  for lead hazards  and conduct  interim  or
abatement  controls  as warranted.  Most of the homes in South Gate were built prior to 1978 and
have lead-based  paint  somewhere  on the structure,  which  is typically  found  on windowsills,
doorways  or under the eaves.  The hazards of lead-based  paint are primarily  for young children
up to age 6, as they are more likely to eat peeling  paint.  Lead adversely  affects the development
of a child's brain and other organs.

The City's strategy  in addressing  lead-based  paint  hazards  involves  an educational  component
for the public,  printed  outreach  information  to those  households  in the "lead  hot zones"  as

rehabilitation  loan programs.

The  City offers  a Residential  Rehabilitation  Program  which  focuses  on rehabilitating  existing

housing stock throughout the City covering interior and exterior home improvement and/or
repairs.  In combination  with  the Residential  Rehabilitation  Program,  the City offers  grants  to be
used for termite  and lead abatement.  Lead assessments  are conducted  on all housing  projects,

both  single  family  and multi-family  units.  Additionally,  all Housing  Choice  Voucher  participant
rental  units are inspected  annually.

The implementation  of CDBG and HOME activities  that will help to reduce  the number  of poverty
level families  include:

  *  Supporting  activities  that  expand  the  supply  of housing  that  is affordable  to  low-and
  moderate-income  households.

  *  Supportingactivitiesthatpreservethesupplyofdecenthousingthatisaffordabletolow-

  Supporting  a continuum  of housing  and public  service  programs  to prevent  and eliminate
  homelessness.

  *  Supporting  housing  preservation  programs  that  assure  low-income  households  have  a
  safe, decent,  and sanitary  place to live; and

  *  Supporting  public  services  for low-and  moderate-income  residents  including  those  with
  special  needs and those  at risk of homelessness  offered  by nonprofit  organizations.

In addition  to these  local  efforts,  mainstream  state  and federal  resources  also contribute  to

reducing  the number  of individuals  and families  in poverty.  In California,  the primary  programs
that  assist  families  in poverty  are CalWORKs,  CalFresh  (formerly  food  stamps)  and  MediCal.

Together,  these  programs  provide  individuals  and families  with  employment  assistance,  subsidies
for  food,  medical  care,  childcare,  and  cash  payments  to  meet  basic  needs  such  as housing,

nutrition,  and  transportation.  Other  services  are  available  to  assist  persons  suffering  from
substance  abuse,  domestic  violence,  and mental  illness.

  SUBJECT:  ORDINANCE  AMENDING  TITLE  9 (BUILDINGS),  OF THE  SOUTH
  GATE  MUNICIPAL  CODE,  IN ITS  ENTIRETY  BY ADOPTING  BY REFERENCE  THE
  2025 EDITION  OF THE  CALIFORNIA  CODES  OF REGULATIONS,  TITLE  24 AND
  THE  2024 EDITION  OF THE  UNIFORM  SOLAR,  HYDRONICS  AND  GEOTHERMAL
  AND  THE  2024 EDITION  OF SWIMMING  POOL,  SPA AND  HOT  TUB  CODES
  PUBLISHED  BY  THE  INTERNATIONAL  ASSOCIATION  OF PLUMBING  AND
  MECHANICAL  OFFICIALS.

  PURPOSE:  To adopt new  State Building  Codes which  are mandated  for statewide  enforcement
  on July 1, 2026.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City  Council  will  consider,  following  the conclusion  of the
  public  hearing,  waiving  the reading  in  fiill  and  introducing  an Ordinance  amending  Title  9
  (Buildings)  of the  South  Gate  Municipal  Code  by  adopting  by reference  the 2025  California
  Code  of Regulations,  Title  24 ("2025  Building  Standards  Code")  and the 2024  International
  Association  of Plumbing  and Mechanical  Officials  Codes,

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  It is estimated  that the cost for staff training  and the purchase  of the 2025
  California  Building  Standards  Code  books  for  City  staff  will  be $7,000.  This  amount  will  be
  expended  from  funds  included  in the FY 2026-2027  Budget  (100-602-42-6305  and 100-602-42-
  6340).

  The new  State Building  Codes  have  significant  changes  from  previous  editions  and will  require
  training  of Building  and Safety  Division  staff,  design  professionals  and contractors  in coming
  months.  Training  on the  new  codes  is currently  available  through  a number  of professional
  associations  including  the International  Code  Council  (ICC),  the International  Association  of
  Plumbing  and  Mechanical  Officials  (IAPMO),  the  International  Association  of  Electrical
  Inspectors  (IAEI),  and the California  Building  Officials  (CALBO).

  ANALYSIS:  In accordance  with  state law, the 2025 Edition  of the California  Building  Standards
  Code was adopted  by the State Building  Standards  Commission  and published  in the California
  Code of Regulations,  Title  24 ("2025  Building  Standards  Code").

  1

  92
 State  law  mandates  that  California  jurisdictions  enforce  the  2025  Building  Standards  Code,
effective  July  1, 2026,  for  all  new  building  constructions  in California.  While  the California
Building  Standards  Commission  adopts  building  code  standards  to  be used  statewide,  City
Council  action  to adopt  these  codes  at a local  level  is also part of the code  adoption  process.
Adoption  of these codes  by the City  allows  for the inclusion  of administrative  provisions  and
limited  amendments  to  the  state  codes.  State  law  permits  local  jurisdictions  to  make
modifications  to  the  state  codes  that  are  reasonably  necessary  because  of  local  conditions
provided  the  City  makes  express  findings  that  the  changes  are needed  because  of  climatic,
geologic  or topographic  conditions.  The  proposed  Ordinance  contains  the  adoption  of these
codes  and administrative  provisions  for  the enforcement  of the codes.  The  Ordinance  makes
findings  regarding  local  geographic,  climatic  and  topographic  conditions  that  make  the
amendments  to the state codes reasonably  necessary  for building  construction  in the City.

In accordance  with  state law, the 2024 Edition  of the Uniform  Swimming  Pool,  Spa and Hot Tub
Code and the 2024 Edition  of the Uniform  Solar,  Hydronics  and Geothermal  Code were adopted
by the State Building  Standards  and published  by the International  Association  of Plumbing  and
Mechanical  Officials.

Administrative  provisions  of the California  Building  Standards  Codes  are adopted  and include
past  amendments  carried  forward  as recommended  by  the  City's  Building  Official.  Such
amendments  include  provisions  regarding  permits,  fees, inspections,  completion  of residential
remodeling  and  Board  of Appeals  proceedings.  The  City  has not  made  any  amendments  to
building,  residential,  plumbing,  electrical  and  mechanical  codes  for  over  thirteen  years.  A
summary  of existing  amendments  carried  forward  are provided  as Attachment  B. Revisions  to
the  California  Building  Code  were  made  to improve  procedures  with  building  permits  and
inspections  as follows:

  *  Clarification  on the expiration  of building  permits  for new  structures  from  180 days to
  365 days.
  *  Clarification  on  the  expiration  of  building  permits  issued  to  legalized  unpermitted
  structures  (60 days).
  *  Clarification  on concealed  work  done without  required  inspection.
  *  Clarification  on requirements  for the issuance  of a certificate  of occupancy.
  *  Clarification  on the release  of utilities.
  *  Clarification  on the process  for legalizing  unpermitted  structures.
  *  Clarification  on the process  for structures  which  cannot  be legalized.

BACKGROUND:  The state's  Building  Standards  Codes  have been subject  to a series of major
transformations  since the 2001  International  Code  Council  (ICC)  model  codes  were introduced.
The new 2025 Building  Standards  Code utilizes  the most up to date code documents  which  have
been developed  through  a national  code development  process.  These  construction  codes include
the California  Administrative,  Building,  Residential,  Electrical,  Plumbing,  Mechanical,  Energy,
Historical  Building,  Existing  Building,  Reference  Standards  and Green  Building  Standards  as
well  as other related  codes.

Adoption  of the proposed  Ordinance  incorporates  the 2025  Building  Standards  Codes  and the
2024  International  Association  of Plumbing  and Mechanical  Officials  (IAPMO)  codes  which
will  keep  the  City's  building  regulations  consistent  with  those  of  the  State.  They  provide

Ordinance  is necessary  to keep us in compliance  with  State regulations  while  allowing  the City
to properly  address  special  local  conditions.

ENVIRONMENTAL  ASSESSMENT:  Environmental  review  is  not  required  under  the
California  Environmental  Quality  Act  (CEQA)  pursuant  to  CEQA  Guidelines  Sections
15060(c)(2)  (the  activity  will  not result  in a direct  or reasonable  foreseeable  indirect  physical

15378),  Title  14, California  Code  of Regulations,  because  adoption  of the proposed  Ordinances
has no potential  for resulting  in a physical  change to the environment,  directly  or indirectly.

each other,  or from  any other electrode,  including  those used for single  circuits,  radio,  telephone,  lighting
rods or any other purpose.

  SUBJECT:  ADOPTION  OF  A  RESOLUTION  ESTABLISHING  A  POLICY  ON
  DISRUPTION  OF REMOTE  PARTICIPATION  DURING  CITY  COUNCIL  MEETINGS
  IN  COMPLIANCE  WITH  SENATE  BILL  707  AND  APPROPRIATING  FUNDS  FOR
  IMPLEMENT  ATION

  PURPOSE:  To establish  a formal  policy  addressing  disruptions  to remote  participation  during
  City  Council  meetings,  as required  by  Senate  Bill  707 (Durazo,  2025)  and Government  Code
  section  54953.4,  and to  establish  procedures  governing  public  comment  and the  conduct  of
  meetings  when  remote  access is disrupted.  The City  Council  will  also consider  an appropriation
  from  the General  Fund  unassigned  fund  balance  to the Information  Systems  Fund  (account  522-
  305-12-6730)  to fund  implementation  of real-time  AI-based  translation  and closed  captioning
  services  required  to support  compliant  remote  public  participation.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Adopting  a Resolution  establishing  a policy  addressing  disruptions  during  remote
  participation  at City  Council  meetings,  in compliance  with  Senate Bill  707.
  b.  Approving  an appropriation  of $41,687.50  from  the General  Fund  unassigned  :tund
  balance  to the  Information  Systems  Fund  (account  522-305-12-6730)  to fund  the
  first-year  subscription  and  one-time  implementation  costs  of  real-time  AI-based
  translation  and closed  captioning  services  in support  of SB 707 compliance.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact  associated  with  the adoption  of the Policy  itself.
  To implement  the real-time  translation  and closed  captioning  services  necessary  to support  SB
  707  compliance,  staff  is requesting  an appropriation  of  $41,687.50  from  the  General  Fund
  unassigned  fund  balance  to the  Information  Systems  Fund  (accoiu'it  522-305-12-6730).  Tis
  amount  covers  the first-year  subscription  cost and one-time  implementation  cost. The anticipated
  total  fiscal  impact  over  a three-year  period  is $60,000,  covering  the  ongoing  costs  of these
  services  (excluding  one-time  implementation  cost).  Staff will  include  the projected  ongoing  costs
  in 'future  fiscal  year budget  submissions  for City  Council  consideration.

  ANALYSIS:  The Ralph  M. Brown  Act requires  that meetings  of local  legislative  bodies  be open
  and accessible  to the public.  Senate  Bill  707 added  Governrnent  Code  section  54953.4,  which

  1  121
 imposes  new  requirements  on "eligible  legislative  bodies."  An  eligible  legislative  body  is
defined  to include  a city  council  of a city with  a population  of 30,000  or more.  The City  of South
Gate, with  a population  of approximately  90,000,  is an eligible  legislative  body  and is therefore
subject  to  these  requirements.  Among  other  things,  section  54953.4  requires  each  eligible
legislative  body,  on or before  July 1, 2026,  to adopt a policy  at a noticed  public  meeting  in open
session,  and not on the consent  calendar,  addressing  disruptions  of telephonic  or internet  service
during  meetings.

The proposed  policy  establishes  the procedures  the City  will  follow  in the event  of a disruption
that prevents  the public  from  attending,  observing,  or participating  in a meeting  via telephonic  or
internet-based  remote  access. The key elements  of the policy  include  the following:

  @  Recessing  the open session  of the meeting  for a minimum  of one hour  or until  service  is
  restored,  whichever  occurs  earlier
  Making  documented  good faith  efforts  to restore  service  pursuant  to a defined  restoration
  checklist,  and providing  public  notice  during  the recess  by website,  social  media,  and
  signage  at City  Hall,  including  in Spanish  when  feasible
  *  Delaying  :[urther  action  on agenda  items  until  remote  public  access  is restored,  with
  actions  taken  in violation  subject  to challenge  under  Government  Code section  54960.1
  *  Allowing  the City  Council  three  options  when  service  cannot  be restored:  (i) continue
  affected  items  to a subsequent  meeting  at a time  and place  certain;  (ii)  adjourn  and re-
  notice;  or (iii)  reconvene  only  after  adopting,  by roll  call  vote,  findings  that  good  faith
  efforts  to restore  service  have  been made  and that the public  interest  in continuing  the
  meeting  outweighs  the public  interest  in remote  meeting  access

Remote  Access  Technology  Implementation
Staff  evaluated  a range  of  remote  participation  platforms,  including  dedicated  governrnent
meeting  solutions  and standalone  telephonic  conferencing  services,  and analyzed  each against
the requirements  of Government  Code  section  54953.4,  cost, integration  with  existing  systems,
staff training  requirements,  and long-term  maintenance.  Staff  recommends  a two-way  telephonic
call-in  option  implemented  through  the  City's  existing  Microso'ft  365  and  Microsoft  Teams
infrastructure.  This  approach  satisfies  the statutory  requirement  for a two-way  telephonic  service,
leverages  infrastructure  the City  already  owns  and staff  already  supports,  avoids  the cost of a
new third-party  platform,  and can be deployed  ahead of the July 1, 2026, operative  date.

In parallel,  staff  will  pilot  Wordly  AI  for  real-time  translation  and interpretation  services  at
Council  meetings,  replacing  the current  reliance  on in-person  interpreters.  Wordly  uses artificial
intelligence  to  provide  simultaneous  interpretation  across  multiple  languages,  delivered  to
attendees  on their  own  mobile  devices,  both  in the Council  Chambers  and to those  attending
remotely.  This  is intended  to produce  a more  consistent  and seamless  experience  for  Spanish-
speaking  residents  and other  language  cornrnunities,  whether  they  attend  in person  or remotely,
and  to  support  the  City's  separate  obligation  under  Governrnent  Code  section  54953.4  to
reasonably  assist members  of the public  who request  interpretation  services.

Public  Comment  Procedures  for Remote  Participation
Consistent  with  the  City's  existing  agenda  language,  comments  from  the  audience  on non-

  2  122
 agenda  items  are limited  to three  (3) minutes  per speaker,  and the collective  initial  period  for
non-agenda  public  cornrnent  is limited  to  45  minutes.  Any  speaker  who  does  not  get  an
opportunity  to speak during  the initial  45-minute  period  due to that time  limitation  will  be given
the opportunity  to speak at the end of the meeting  prior  to adjournment.

Under  the practice  recommended  in this  staff report,  speakers  attending  in person  will  be heard
first,  followed  by  speakers  participating  remotely  by  telephonic  service.  This  sequencing  is
intended  to preserve  the orderly  conduct  of the meeting  while  the City  transitions  to a hybrid
public  comment  format.  To  ensure  consistency  with  Government  Code  section  54953.4,  the
following  safeguards  will  apply:  (a) the 45-minute  cap applies  to the combined  queue  of in-
person  and remote  speakers;  (b) remote  speakers  who  are in the queue at the time  the 45-minute
cap is reached  will  be guaranteed  the opportunity  to speak  at the end of the meeting  prior  to
adjournment,  in the order they joined  the queue;  (c) the remote  telephonic  platform  shall remain
active  through  the end-of-meeting  public  cornrnent  opportunity;  and (d) the sequencing  rule shall
not  be used  to  defer  any  speaker  who  has identified  a disability-based  need  to participate
remotely,  who shall be heard in turn with  in-person  speakers.

Staff  notes  that  Goverent  Code  section  54953.4  requires  that  remote  public  comments  be
offered  in real time  and prohibits  requiring  comments  to be submitted  in advance.  The in-person-
first  sequencing  described  above  represents  a good  faith  effort  to balance  orderly  meeting
administration  with  the statutory  right  to real-time  remote  comment  and is supported  by the end-
of-meeting  guarantee  for deferred  remote  speakers.  Staff  will  monitor  the experience  during  the
first  few  months  of  implementation  and return  to the  City  Council  with  any  recommended
adjustments,  if any. The City  Attorney  has reviewed  the public  comment  sequencing  procedure.

Related  SB 707 Compliance  Items
Adoption  of this  policy  is one of  several  actions  required  under  Government  Code  section
54953.4  by July  1, 2026.  Staff  is separately  preparing  the following  related  items  for  Council
consideration  in advance  of that deadline:  (1) implementation  of the two-way  telephonic  remote
participation  option  through  Microsoft  Teams;  (2) translation  of meeting  agendas  into applicable
languages,  including  Spanish;  (3)  a dedicated  public  meetings  webpage  with  participation
instructions,  a meeting  calendar,  and outreach  materials;  (4) written  procedures  for processing
disability  accommodation  requests  for  remote  participation;  and  (5)  outreach  to  community
organizations  and non-English-speaking  media  to invite  participation  in public  meetings.  Staff

Adoption  of this  policy  ensures  the  City  remains  compliant  with  SB  707  while  maintaining
transparency  and public  participation.

  POLICY:  DISRUPTION  OF REMOTE  PARTICIPATION  DURING
  CITY  COUNCIL  MEETINGS  AND  PUBLIC  COMMENT  DURING
  REMOTE  PARTICIPATION

  1. PURPOSE
  This Policy  establishes  procedures  for addressing  disruptions  to telephonic  or internet-
  based remote  participation  during  City  Council  meetings,  in compliance  with
  Government  Code section  54953.4,  enacted  by Senate Bill  707 (Durazo,  2025)  and the
  Ralph  M. Brown  Act.  This Policy  also establishes  procedures  governing  public  comment
  during  meetings  at which  remote  participation  is offered,  to ensure consistent
  administration  of public  cornrnent  rights  for members  of the public  attending  in person
  and those attending  remotely.

  2. APPLICABILITY
  This Policy  applies  to all meetings  of the City  Council  of the City  of South  Gate where
  remote  participation  is provided  through  telephonic  or audiovisual  platforms.  The City
  Council  may, by motion  or resolution,  extend  this Policy  to other City  legislative  bodies,
  boards,  commissions,  and cornrnittees  that provide  remote  public  participation.

  3. POLICY
  The City  of South  Gate shall ensure that members  of the public  are provided  with
  meaningful  access to participate  in City  Council  meetings,  including  the ability  to attend
  and provide  public  comments  remotely  when  such access is offered.

  4. PROCEDURES  FOR  DISRUPTION  OF REMOTE  ACCESS
  a. Identification  of Disruption

  A disruption  occurs  when  telephonic  or internet-based  services  prevent  members
  of the public  from  attending,  observing,  or participating  in the meeting  via the
  two-way  telephonic  service  or two-way  audiovisual  platform.  The City  Clerk,  or
  designee,  in coordination  with  the Information  Technology  (IT)  Division,  shall be
  responsible  for identifying  and confirming  a disruption  and promptly  notifying  the
  presiding  officer.

  b. Recess  of Meeting

  In the event of a disruption,  the City  Council  shall recess the open session  of the
  meeting  for a minimum  of one (1) hour or until  telephonic  or internet  service  is
  restored,  whichever  occurs  earlier.  During  the recess, the City  Clerk  and IT

  128
 Division,  in coordination  with  affected  vendors,  shall make a good faith  effort  to
restore  service,  which  may include,  as applicable:  (i) verifying  internet
connectivity  and network  status; (ii) restarting  the streaming  platform  and call-in
bridge;  (iii)  activating  backup  internet  or cellular  hotspot  service;  (iv) rebooting
audiovisual  equipment;  and (v) contacting  platform  or service  provider  technical
support.  The City  Clerk  shall document  the nature  of the disruption,  the time  it
was identified,  each restoration  step attempted,  and the outcome,  and shall  cause
the documentation  to be retained  as part of the meeting  record.

c. Public  Notice  During  Recess

During  the recess, the City  Clerk  shall make reasonable  efforts  to inform  the
public  of the disniption  and the expected  time  of reconvening.  Reasonable  efforts
may include  posting  notice  on the City's  website  and official  social  media
channels,  posting  physical  notice  at City  Hall,  and, when feasible,  providing
notice  in Spanish  and other applicable  languages.

d. Restoration  of Sewice

If telephonic  or internet  service  is restored  during  the recess, the City  Council
shall reconvene  the open session  of the meeting  and resume  the agenda.

e. Inability  to Restore  Sewice

If telephonic  or internet  service  has not been restored  following  the recess, the
City  Council  shall choose  one of the following  options:

  i. Continue  the affected  agenda items  to a subsequent  meeting  at a time
  and place certain,  announced  on the record  and posted  as required  by law;
  or

  ii. Adjourn  the meeting  and renotice  the remaining  agenda items  as
  required  by law;  or

  iii. Reconvene  the open session of the meeting  only  after adopting  the
  findings  described  below.

To reconvene  the open session  under  option  (iii),  the City  Council  shall adopt,  by
roll  call vote, findings  that:

  (1) good faith  efforts  to restore  the telephonic  or internet  service  have been
  made in accordance  with  this Policy;  and

  (2) the public  interest  in continuing  the meeting  outweighs  the public
  interest  in remote  meeting  access.

  129
   The findings  shall be recorded  in the meeting  minutes,  together  with  the
  documentation  prepared  pursuant  to subsection  (b).

  f. Limitation  on Actions

  During  any disruption  that prevents  the City  Council  from  broadcasting  the
  meeting  to the public  or that prevents  the public  from  offering  public  comment
  through  the remote  platform,  the City  Council  shall take no further  action  on
  items  appearing  on the meeting  agenda until  public  access is restored  or until  the
  findings  described  in subsection  (e) have been adopted.  Actions  taken in violation
  of this subsection  may be challenged  pursuant  to Government  Code section
  54960.1.

5. CLOSED  SESSION
The City  Council  may meet in closed  session  during  the recess period  described  in
Section  4, consistent  with  Government  Code section  54953.4  and other applicable
provisions  of the Brown  Act.

6. IMPLEMENT  ATION
The City  Clerk,  in coordination  with  the Information  Technology  Division,  shall
implement  and monitor  this Policy.  The City  Manager  is authorized  to adopt
administrative  procedures  consistent  with  this Policy,  including  a written  disruption
response  checklist,  designation  of primary  and backup  monitoring  personnel,  staff
training,  and periodic  testing  of restoration  procedures

7. PUBLIC  COMMENT  DURING  REMOTE  PARTICIPATION
  a. Time  Limits

  Cornrnents  from  the audience  on non-agenda  items  shall be limited  to three (3)
  minutes  per speaker.  Unless  authorized  by the Mayor,  the time limit  may not be
  extended  by utilizing  another  member's  time.  The collective  initial  period  for
  non-agenda  public  comment  shall be limited  to forty-five  (45) minutes.  Any
  speaker  who does not get an opportunity  to speak during  the initial  45-minute
  period  due to that time  limitation  shall be given  the opportunity  to speak at the
  end of the meeting  prior  to adjournment.

  b. Order  of Speakers

  During  the initial  45-minute  public  comment  period,  members  of the public
  attending  the meeting  in person  shall be heard first,  in the order in which  they
  submit  speaker  cards or are recognized  by the presiding  officer.  Members  of the
  public  participating  remotely  by telephonic  or audiovisual  platform  shall be heard
  after in-person  speakers,  in the order they join  the remote  speaker  queue.

  130
   c. Safeguards  for Remote  Participants

  To ensure consistency  with  Government  Code section  54953.4  and the right  to
  real-time  public  comment,  the following  safeguards  shall apply:

  i. The 45-minute  cap in subsection  (a) shall apply  to the combined  queue
  of in-person  and remote  speakers.

  ii. Remote  speakers  who  are in the queue at the time the 45-minute  cap is
  reached  shall be guaranteed  the opportunity  to speak at the end of the
  meeting  prior  to adjournment,  in the order they joined  the queue.

  iii. The remote  telephonic  or audiovisual  platform  shall remain  active
  through  the end-of-meeting  public  comment  opportunity

  iv. The sequencing  rule in subsection  (b) shall not be used to defer any
  speaker  who has identified  a disability-based  need to participate  remotely,
  who shall be heard in turn with  in-person  speakers.

  d. Real-Time  Comment;  No Pre-Submission  Required

  Members  of the public  shall not be required  to submit  comments  in advance  of the
  meeting,  and shall be provided  the opportunity  to address the City  Council  in real
  time,  whether  attending  in person  or remotely.

  e. Decorum

  There  shall be no debate or action  on items not listed  on the agenda unless
  authorized  by law. The presiding  officer  may remove  or limit  the participation  of
  any member  of the public,  whether  attending  in person  or remotely,  who actually
  disrupts,  disturbs,  impedes,  or renders  infeasible  the orderly  conduct  of the
  meeting,  consistent  with  Government  Code sections  54957.95  and 54957.96  and
  South  Gate Municipal  Code section  1.04.110.

8. EFFECTIVE  DATE
This Policy  is effective  upon adoption  and shall apply  to all City  Council  meetings  held
on or after July 1, 2026.

  PARKING  AND  BUSINESS  IMPROVEMENT  AREA

  ANNUAL  REPORT  FOR  FISCAL  YEAR  2026/27

 This annual report  includes  the proposed  assessment  levy and program  budget  for the fiscal  year

 2026/27.

 Tweedy  Mile  Advisory  Board
 Per the Parking  and Business  Improvement  Area  Law  of 1989  and the South  Gate Municipal
 Code,  Chapter  2.64,  the City  Council  shall  appoint  a Tweedy  Mile  Advisory  Board  in order to
 make recommendations  to the City  Council  on the expendihire  of revenues  derived  from  the levy
 assessments  on proposed  improvements  and activities  and on the method  and basis  of levying
 assessments.

 Purpose  of Annual  Report
 The Tweedy  Mile  Advisory  Board  shall prepare  an annual  report  for each fiscal  year for which
 assessments  are to be levied  and collected  to pay the costs of the improvements  and activities
 described  in the report.  The  report  may  propose  changes,  including  but  not  limited  to, the
 boundaries  of the parking  and business  improvement  area and the basis and method  of levying
 the assessments.

 Boundaries  and Assessments
 There  are no proposed  changes  to the  Parking  and  Business  Improvement  Area  ("Area")
 boundaries  or  the  assessment  methodology.  The  Area  boundary  map  and  assessment
 methodology  are included  as Exhibits  A and B.

 Method  and Basis  of Levying  the Assessment
 All  businesses  within  the Area  are subject  to the assessment.  The levy  of the business  license
 tax imposed  upon  the businesses  within  said Area,  is hereby  fixed,  levied,  determined,  and
 established  per the City's  assessment  methodology  included  with  this  report  as Exhibit  B.

 Payment  of Tax
 The additional  rate or levy  of the license  tax levied  is due and payable  at the same time  and in
 the same manner  that the business  license  tax is imposed  by the South  Gate Municipal  Code
 Chapter  2.08 (Business  License  Tax).

Budqet
The proposed  budget  for  Fiscal  Year  2026/27  is included  in the Annual  Report.  Funding  is
anticipated  to be used for the installation,  removal,  and storage  of seasonal  decorations  along
Tweedy  Blvd.,  subject  to further  Board  evaluation  and  approval.  Approximately  $48,510  is
expected  to support  these decoration-related  costs.  The Board  will  review  and approve  specific
funding  requests  in the next Fiscal  Year.

  PURPOSE:  To adopt  Resolutions  to preliminarily  approve  the Engineer's  Report,  to declare
  the City  of South  Gate's  ("City")  intention  to levy  and collect  assessments,  and to set a public
  hearing.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Adopting  a Resolution  preliminarily  approving  the Engineer's  Report  for the proceedings
  of the Fiscal  Year  2026/27  Annual  Levy  and Collection  of Assessments  for  the Street
  Lighting  and Landscape  Maintenance  District  No. 1; and
  b.  Adopting  a Resolution  declaring  the  City's  intention  to levy  and  collect  assessments
  under  the Fiscal  Year  2026/27  Annual  Levy  and Collection  of Assessments  within  the
  Street  Lighting  and Landscape  Maintenance  District  No. 1 and setting  a Public  Hearing
  for May  26, 2026.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  The  cost  of  preparing  the  Engineer's  Report  is $8,660  and  it  will  be
  funded  with  Street  Lighting  and  Landscaping  Funds  budgeted  in  the  Fiscal  Year  2026/27
  Municipal  Budget.

  ANALYSIS:  The  assessment  rate  is set at $2.38  per  adjusted  front  footage.  Although  the
  revenue  from  this  assessment  has remained  the  same  for  nearly  three  decades,  the  cost  of
  maintaining  the District  has risen,  creating  a funding  shortfall.  For FY  2026/27,  the revenue  is
  estimated  at $1,993,942,  while  maintenance  costs  are estimated  at $3,041,636,  resulting  in a
  budget  deficit  of $1,225,016.

  In April  2016,  the City  Council  authorized  an analysis  to explore  ways  to address  the fiinding
  shortfall,  including  the  possibility  of  raising  the  assessment  rate  through  a Proposition  218
  process,  which  requires  property  owner  approval  for any new or increased  assessments.  At that
  time,  the consultant  found  that while  raising  the rate in the existing  District  could  help,  creating

 new districts  would  be a more  effective  way to generate  additional  funds,  and staff did not move
forward  with  a Proposition  218 effort.

BACKGROUND:  The District  was established  in 1981  and operates  iu'ider  the Landscaping
and  Lighting  Act  of  1972  (California  Streets  and  Highways  Code).  This  law  provides  the
authority  to levy  an assessment  on properties  that receive  a direct  "special  benefit"  from  public
improvements,  such as landscaping  and street lighting.  Since the District  covers  the entire  City,
the assessment  is levied  on all properties  throughout  the City.

To remain  compliance  with  the rules of the district,  District  revenue  can only  be used to maintain
and  operate  landscaping  and  lighting  systems  throughout  the  City  and  on City  streets.  This
includes  expenses  for  landscaping  (trees,  shrubs,  grass,  irrigation,  and drainage)  and lighting
systems  (streetlights,  decorative  fixtures,  traffic  signals,  and related  equipment),  including  labor
and materials.

Each  year,  the  District's  assessments  are levied  and  collected  by  the  Los  Angeles  County
Assessor's  Office  ("County")  on behalf  of the City  through  the property  tax roll.  In order  for the
County  to levy  and collect  the assessments,  the City  Council  must take certain  actions  required
by the County  and in accordance  with  applicable  state law.  The  actions  presented  to the City
Council  are part  of the  annual  proceedings  necessary  to authorize  the  County  to place  the
assessments  on the tax roll  and collect  them on behalf  of the City.

On  January  13,  2026,  the  City  Council  adopted  Resolution  No.  2026-01-CC  to  initiate
proceedings  for  FY  2026/27  and directed  the preparation  of the Engineer's  Report.  The  next
steps in the process  can be completed  by adopting  the two proposed  resolutions  before  the City
Council,  which  will  achieve  the following:

  *  Declare  the City's  intention  to levy  and collect  assessments  in FY  2026/27  within  the
  District;

  *  Set a public  hearing  for May  26, 2026.  At that time,  the City  Council  will,  (a) consider
  and determine  whether  to levy  the proposed  annual  assessment,  and (b) hear all protests
  related  to (i) said proposed  proceedings,  (ii)  the estimate  of the cost and expenses  of the
  proposed  maintenance,  and/or  (iii)  the proposed  annual  assessment.  Any  and all persons
  interested  may  file  a written  protest  prior  to the conclusion  of the hearing  referred  to
  herein;  and

  *  Preliminarily  approved  the Engineer's  Report  which  is the document  required  to set the
  amount  of the assessment.  The Engineer's  Report  contains  a description  of the District,
  District  budget,  an analysis  of revenue  needs,  a benefit  analysis,  the total  parcels  located
  within  the District,  and the amount  to be assessed.

improvements  are considered  a special  benefit  to adjacent  properties.  Funding  for maintenance

SUBJECT:  AMENDMENTOFTHECITY'S"LOWIMPACTDEVELOPMENTTECHNICAI,
  GUIDAJSJCE  MANUAL  FOR  SMALL  SITES  PURSUANT  TO  SOUTH  GATE
  MUNICIP  AL  CODE  SECTION  6.67.030,  SUBSECTION  E.4.G.

PURPOSE:  To modify  the "Low  Impact  Development  Technical  Guidance  Manual  for Small  Sites"  in
order to expand  the current  exemption  for projects  of 800 square feet or less to the larger,  state-authorized
exemption  for projects  of 5,000 square feet or less.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider  adopting  a Resolution  to modify  the
Low  Impact  Development  Technical  Guidance  Manual  for Small  Sites to expand  the current  exemption
from the City's  Low  Impact  Development  (LID)  Program  forprojects  of 800 square feet or less to the larger,
state-authorized  exemption  for projects  of 5,000 square feet or less.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  None.

ANALYSIS:  TheCityacceptsdevelopmentapplicationsfornewdevelopmentandredevelopmentprojects.
Currently,  projects  involving  soil disturbance  of 800 square feet or more  are required  to comply  with  the
City's  Low  Impact  Development  (LID)  Program.  This  threshold  is more  stringent  than  the  State
requirement,  which  applies  to projects  involving  5,000  square feet or more  of soil disturbance.

There  is interest  in revising  the City's  threshold  to align  with  the State standard  in order  to streamline
development  review,  reduce  project  costs,  and make  development  in South  Gate more  attractive  and
affordable.  Requiring  LID  compliance  for smaller  projects  is o'ftennot  cost-effective  and canplace  anundue
burden  on applicants.  In addition,  there  is no clear  direct  benefit  to the City  from  maintaining  a more
stringent  local threshold,  particularly  when it may have the unintended  effect  of discouraging  development.
Accordingly,  staff recommends  amending  the City's  LID threshold  from  800 square feetto  5,000 square feet
to align with  State requirements.

BACKGROUND:  The City  operates  under  an MS4  Stormwater  Permit  ("Permit"),  which  regulates  the
discharge  of stormwater  runoff  from  the municipal  separate  storm  sewer  system  and requires  the City  to
implement  programs  to reduce  pollutants  in stormwater  to the maximum  extent  practicable.

  t  161
 The Permit  requires  the City  to implement  a Low  Impact  Development  (LID)  program.  This  program
requires  that  new  development  and redevelopment  projects  incorporate  design  features  that  infiltrate,
capture,  treat, or reuse stormwater  runoff  to reduce  pollutant  loads and mimic  natural  hydrology.

The City's  OrdinanceNo.  2310 establishes  requirementsfor"Small  SiteNewDevelopment/Redevelopment
Pollutant  Reduction,"  including  the requirement  to prepare  and implement  a Low  Impact  Development
Technical  Guidance  Manual  for Small  Sites (LID  Manual).

The City's  LID  Manual  states that projects  resulting  in the creation,  addition,  or replacement  of 800 square
feet or more  of impervious  surface  area must  be designed  to control  pollutants  in accordance  with  the
Manual.  Projects  that trigger  this threshold  are required  to prepare  a LID  Plan.

The State requires  the City to implement  an LID  program;  however,  the State threshold  for requiring  LID
measures  is 5,000 square feet of impervious  surface.  It is unclear  why South Gate adopted  a more stringent
local threshold  of 800 square feet, but that lower  threshold  has proven  to be burdensome  on development
projects  and, in some cases, unnecessarily  restrictive.

South  Gate Municipal  Code  Section  6.67.030,  subsection  E.4.g,  authorizes  the City  Council  to adopt
resolutions  to modify  the Manual  and create or modify  exceptions  thereto.  The City  Council  is therefore
authorized  to modify  the Manual  to increase  the exception  threshold  from  800 square feet to 5,000 square
feet.  Staff recommends  that the City  Council  adopt the attached  Resolution  to increase  that threshold.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider  re-appropriating  $400,000  in

  Contract  No. C5055034;  State Project  No.  SG-19-105)  to the Hollydale  Community  Park Project

  appropriation  is budgeted  in the FY 2025/26  Capital  Improvement  Program.

  ANALYSIS:  Following  the  receipt  of  over  $13.4M  in  grant  funds,  the  City  initiated
  construction  of  the  Hollydale  Community  Park  Renovation  Project  and  the  Circle  Park
  Renovation  Project.  The grant funds were fully  appropriated  and allocated  between  both projects
  to support  their  implementation.

  need to reallocate  $400,000  in State Department  of Parks  and Recreation  grant  funds  from  the

 SUBJECT:  PURCHASE  OF TWELVE  (12) MOBILE  DATA  COMPUTERS  (MDC)
 FOR  POLICE  VEHICLES

 PURPOSE:  To purchase  twelve  (12) Mobile  Data Computers  (MDC)  to replace  the aging,
 malfunctioning  and end-of-life  units installed  in Police  Vehicles.

 RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Authorizing  the purchase  of twelve  (12) Mobile  Data Computer  (MDC)  units  in the total
  amount  of $77,373.34,  which  includes  hardware,  five  (5) years of extended  warranty,
  field  engineering  support,  and deployment/installation  services;  and
  b.  Authorizing  the City  Manager,  or his designee,  to execute  all documents  necessary  to
  complete  the purchases  in a form  acceptable  to the City Attorney.

 FISCAL  IMPACT:  Funding  for this purchase  was approved  in the Fiscal  Year 2025/2026  budget
 under  account  number  522-310-12-9006.  The  original  budget  allocation  anticipated  the
 replacement  of eight (8) MDC  units at an estimated  cost of $10,000  per unit.  Through  competitive
 pricing,  the Department  secured  twelve  (12) MDC  units  at approximately  $5,087  per unit,  along
 with  associated  equipment,  warranties,  and support  services.

 ANALYSIS:  The  South  Gate  Police  Department's  MDC  units  in each patrol  vehicle  is an
 essential  and critical  component  to all sworn  duty  personnel.  Such systems  contribute  to daily
 police  operations,  enabling  sworn  personnel  to  access  dispatch  systems,  law  enforcement
 databases,  and real-time  communication  tools  while  in the field.  Reliable  MDC  functionality  is
 essential  to ensure timely  response  to public  safety  incidents.

 The current  MDC  units  are approximately  five  (5) to six (6) years  old, approaching  end of life.
 Such units are ineligible  for hardware  upgrades  or manufacturer  support  due to outdated  hardware
 specifications.  Due to the nature  of addressing  public  safety  in a quick  and responsive  manner,  it
 is imperative  that all sworn  personnel  possess  effective  tools  necessary  to respond,  mitigate  and
 resolve  threats.  Operating  on  aging  MDC  produces  such  issues  as:  failing  or  internupted
 connectivity  to the Los Angeles  Sheriffs  Department,  failing  or internipted  connectivity  to South
 Gate Police  Department's  dispatch  center,  inability  to effectively  access agency  related  data in the
 field  and hindering  data processing

  1
  195
 Aging  MDC  units  also  pose  the  risk  of  no  longer  receiving  firmware  updates  from  the
manufacturer  which  drives  every  hardware  component  of the unit,  operating  system  incapability
with  said hardware  and exposing  such units  to security  vulnerabilities  and exploits.  MDC  units
that  are no longer  able to receive  manufacturing  support  and/or  updates  along  with  Windows
Operating  System updates expose  the South Gate  Police  Department  and any  data thereof  to
potential cyberattacks and malicious  threat actors.

Such practices  of upgrading  MDC  units are not independent  to South Gate Police  Department,  but
rather  such is an information  technology  industry  standard  of consistently  refreshing  MDC's  that
is practiced  throughout  other law  enforcement  agencies.  Refreshing  MDC  units  on a five  (5) to
seven  (7) year basis ensures  that not only  does the South  Gate Police  Department  operate  with
computing  equipment  that is current  and supported  by operating  system  developers  and hardware
manufacturers,  but such practices  indirectly  contribute  to solidifying  and protecting  the overall
City's  cybersecurity  posture.  As  aforementioned,  outdated  and unsupported  hardware  for  any
computing  device  exposes  said  device  to  vulnerabilities,  exploits  contributing  to  potential
compromising  actions  from  non-authorized  users.

While  adhering  to information  security  and information  technology  industry  standards  may  be
preferred  and  seen as ideal,  South  Gate  Police  Department  must  adhere  to CJIS  compliance
concerning  computing  technology  and the maintenance  thereof.  Compliance  with  Criminal  Justice
Information  Services  (CJIS)  requirements  mandates  that  all  computing  systems  meet  current
security  standards.  MDCs  must support  modern  encryption  protocols,  mobile  device  management
(MDM)  compatibility,  and hardware-based  security  features  such as disk encryption.  CJIS Policy
Section  SA-22  requires  agencies  to replace  unsupported  system  components  or provide  continued
vendor  support.  The Department's  existing  MDC  units no longer  meet these requirements,  placing
the City  at risk of non-compliance.

BACKGROUND:  Following  a comprehensive  assessment  conducted  during  Fiscal  Year
2025/2026,  the Technical  Services  Manager  determined  that the current  MDC  units  are no longer
viable  for operational  use and will  not meet upcoming  CJIS compliance  standards  or align  with
National  Institute  of Standards  and Technology  (NIST)  and Center  for  Internet  Security  (CIS)
guidelines.

To  maintain  operational  readiness,  ensure  regulatory  compliance,  and  support  public  safety
personnel,  it is recommended  that the City proceed  with the replacement  of the existing  MDC  units
utilizing  the approved  budget.
